summary: A reel or post shared into an Instagram group is no longer invisible to Nora, and she can read someone's story.
details: Until now a shared reel arrived with nothing in it — no words, no picture — and was discarded. She did not fail to read it; she never learned anybody had posted anything. Now the caption and the account it came from arrive as text, and the thumbnail arrives as a picture she can look at if asked.

Reading the caption and the author costs nothing at all: both already arrive with the message. A room where people share reels all day is therefore free to follow. Only a direct question about one particular post costs anything, and only then does she look at the picture or the video.

The bridge does not try to say whether a shared thing is a reel, a post or a profile. Instagram's own labels are passed through untouched, because guessing the categories would read as if they had been checked.
Who shared it and who posted it are kept apart. Saying a member of the room made a stranger's reel is the mistake that would look most like a correct answer.
Stories can now be read, and this is the only way to read one — the other tool can only post a story, not look at one.

A story read tells its author that Nora watched, so the route reads exactly one person at a time and never a batch, and there is a free way to check whether somebody has a story at all before looking.
limitations: Nothing calls the story route yet. Nora's side still points at the old location, so asking her for someone's story still fails until that is rewired.

The shape of a shared post has never been captured from a live message, so the fields are read defensively from both of the two possible spellings. A real one may still arrive in a shape that produces a thinner line than it should.

Whether she can read a particular person's story is decided by Instagram, not by Nora: a private account she follows is readable in full, one she does not follow returns nothing. An empty answer says which of those it was rather than reporting a refusal as 'they posted nothing'.
